(CNN) -- Kate Meinhardt felt like a clown jammed into a Volkswagen bug when she lived in a 21-square-foot room aboard a circus train. Kate Meinhardt crammed her life into a 21-square-foot room while she lived aboard a circus train. Bungee cords crisscrossed her walls once a week to prevent an avalanche of items from raining down. A microwave, mini refrigerator, her laptop and baskets of personal items lined the dorm-like room. Showering, going to the bathroom and even doing laundry became racing contests on the train, Meinhardt said. The 13 people on board shared one shower, two toilets and one washer and dryer. "It's a pretty tough life living in such a small space," she said. The 23-year-old spent almost a year as an animal handler for Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey Circus. While most iReporters haven't run off to join the circus, some have traded in their homes for smaller digs. One iReporter even opted for a floating lifestyle, where he could sail away at a moment's notice. iReport.com: Living in tight quarters . Living on a 25-foot boat was only supposed to be temporary, but Jim Smith loved it so much he stayed there for a year. "I have lived in a 25-foot sailboat, a 28-foot motor home, a 32-foot sailboat and now an 800 square-foot apartment," Smith said in his iReport. "I was happiest with the 25-foot sailboat." While docked in Panama City, Florida, Smith kept his expenses to a minimum. The marina slip rent was only $200 and electricity was included in the rent, he said. The boat did not have refrigeration so Smith kept his food inside an insulated ice box. For 79 cents at the discount grocery store, he could buy a 10-pound bag of ice that would last him several days, even during the summer. Air conditioning wasn't a luxury Smith had either, but fans and sea breezes kept him cool. "Sometimes the less you have, the more you like it," he said. The portable lifestyle also charmed a father-son duo who set out on a yearlong European vacation. A camper van took them wherever they wanted, whenever they wanted. Spencer Pearson and his 15-year-old son, Bryce, bought a 150-square-foot van in Germany for their European excursion. Living out of the van meant "no reservations, no packing and unpacking of suitcases, no strange beds," Pearson said. Modern amenities weren't amiss on the van, which included everything from the Internet and entertainment to a complete bath and kitchen, and there were occasional hotel stays and meals out that made the trip more pleasant. The simple life also enticed Deborah Greant and her husband to trade in their Calgary, Canada, home for an RV. Both she and her husband have neuromuscular problems and needed extra help taking care of their large home. Since moving into a 240-square-foot RV, they can manage the house themselves. "We didn't want to be owned by our things," Greant said. "We jettisoned pretty much everything except things from former generations." While two people living in an RV can be tight, imagine a family of six trying to do the same. Mounting living expenses and a job relocation prompted the Chervenkas to sell their home and move into a 32-foot RV. Two pets came along, too. The Chervenkas weren't forced to do this. Their goal was to become debt-free and save money for their children's college educations. When pilot Tim Chervenka got transferred to Charlotte, North Carolina, the family set up camp in a 32-foot RV. The temporary situation turned into a permanent one. The family said goodbye to paying a first and second mortgage and pricey utilities. They now pay only $500 a month, utilities included. "It's made such an adjustment in our personal life without the juggling," Cindy Chervenka said. "We have so much more family time. It's a good feeling." Cindy Chervenka has some advice for others thinking of a drastic downsizing: "Step out of your comfort zone and try it. We didn't plan on doing this full-time, but once we discovered it, we thought, 'hey we can do this forever!' Until you step out and try it, you'll think it's not doable."

Meinhardt packed her entire life into the tiny, dorm-like space. Once a week, bungee cords crisscrossed her walls to keep an avalanche of belongings from tumbling down. A microwave, mini refrigerator, laptop, and baskets of personal items lined the room.

On the train, even showering, using the bathroom, and doing laundry became races, Meinhardt said. The 13 people on board shared one shower, two toilets, and one washer and dryer.

“It’s a pretty tough life living in such a small space,” she said.

The 23-year-old spent nearly a year as an animal handler for Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey Circus.

While most iReporters have not run off to join the circus, some have traded traditional homes for smaller quarters. One iReporter even chose a floating lifestyle, allowing him to sail away at a moment’s notice.

iReport.com: Living in tight quarters

Living on a 25-foot boat was supposed to be temporary, but Jim Smith enjoyed it so much that he stayed for a year.

“I have lived in a 25-foot sailboat, a 28-foot motor home, a 32-foot sailboat and now an 800 square-foot apartment,” Smith said in his iReport. “I was happiest with the 25-foot sailboat.”

While docked in Panama City, Florida, Smith kept his expenses to a minimum. Marina slip rent was only $200, with electricity included, he said. Because the boat had no refrigeration, Smith stored his food in an insulated ice box. For 79 cents at a discount grocery store, he could buy a 10-pound bag of ice that lasted several days, even in summer.

Air conditioning was not among Smith’s comforts, either, but fans and sea breezes kept him cool.

“Sometimes the less you have, the more you like it,” he said.

A portable lifestyle also appealed to a father-son duo who set out on a yearlong European vacation. A camper van took them wherever they wanted to go, whenever they wished.

Spencer Pearson and his 15-year-old son, Bryce, bought a 150-square-foot van in Germany for their European excursion. Living out of the van meant “no reservations, no packing and unpacking of suitcases, no strange beds,” Pearson said.

The van was not lacking in modern amenities: it included everything from Internet access and entertainment to a full bath and kitchen. Occasional hotel stays and meals out made the trip even more enjoyable.

The simple life also drew Deborah Greant and her husband to exchange their Calgary, Canada, home for an RV. Both have neuromuscular problems and had needed extra help maintaining their large house. Since moving into a 240-square-foot RV, they have been able to manage the home themselves.

“We didn’t want to be owned by our things,” Greant said. “We jettisoned pretty much everything except things from former generations.”

While two people living in an RV can feel crowded, imagine a family of six doing the same.

Rising living expenses and a job relocation prompted the Chervenkas to sell their home and move into a 32-foot RV. Two pets came along as well.

The Chervenkas were not forced into the decision. Their goal was to become debt-free and save money for their children’s college educations. When pilot Tim Chervenka was transferred to Charlotte, North Carolina, the family set up camp in the RV. What began as a temporary arrangement became permanent.

The family said goodbye to paying both a first and second mortgage, along with costly utilities. They now pay only $500 a month, utilities included.

“It’s made such an adjustment in our personal life without the juggling,” Cindy Chervenka said. “We have so much more family time. It’s a good feeling.”

Cindy Chervenka offers this advice to others considering a dramatic downsizing: “Step out of your comfort zone and try it. We didn’t plan on doing this full-time, but once we discovered it, we thought, ‘Hey, we can do this forever!’ Until you step out and try it, you’ll think it’s not doable.”

# Big lives, tiny homes: Why some Americans are choosing to live with less

By Staff Writer

When the circus train rolled into a new city, Marcus Hale knew exactly how much room he had to call home: a narrow bunk, a small locker and just enough space to turn around.

For nearly a decade, Hale worked behind the scenes with a traveling circus, sleeping in a train car as the show moved from town to town. His “apartment” was smaller than many walk-in closets. But to him, it was also freedom.

“You learn pretty quickly what you actually need,” he said. “A few changes of clothes, good boots, a place to sleep and people you trust nearby.”

Across the country, a growing number of Americans are rethinking the meaning of home. Some are driven by rising housing costs. Others are chasing flexibility, adventure or a simpler way of life. Their homes may be tiny — train compartments, boats, camper vans and recreational vehicles — but the lives unfolding inside them are often anything but small.

## A life measured in miles, not square feet

Hale’s days on the circus train began early and ended late. He helped move equipment, repair rigging and prepare the venue before performers stepped into the lights. His home followed him from city to city, rattling through the night while he slept.

Privacy was limited. Storage was almost nonexistent. Showers and meals were shared. But Hale said the tight quarters created a sense of community he had never found in a traditional apartment.

“When everyone lives that close, you can’t hide who you are,” he said. “You become family fast.”

The tradeoff was constant motion. Birthdays, holidays and bad days happened on the rails. Hale missed weddings and family dinners. But he also saw more of the country than he ever imagined.

“I didn’t have a living room,” he said. “But I had sunrises in places I’d never have gone otherwise.”

## Home, floating at the dock

For boat dwellers like Elena Ruiz, home comes with tides, weather reports and the steady creak of lines against the dock.

Ruiz moved onto a 34-foot sailboat after a rent increase forced her to reconsider life in a coastal city. At first, she imagined it as a temporary solution. Years later, she still wakes up to gulls overhead and coffee brewed in a galley barely wide enough for one person.

“Everything on a boat has a purpose,” Ruiz said. “If something comes in, something else usually has to go out.”

Living aboard means learning to conserve water, fix leaks and watch the sky. A storm can turn a quiet night into hours of checking ropes and listening for trouble. Laundry is done onshore. Groceries must be carried carefully down the dock. Guests are welcome, but not many at once.

Still, Ruiz said the rewards outweigh the inconveniences.

“I know my neighbors. I know the weather. I know the sound of my own home,” she said. “There’s something grounding about that, even when you’re floating.”

## The open road as a front porch

For couples traveling by camper van, the appeal is often not just affordability but mobility.

Jenna and Miles Porter converted a used cargo van into a compact home with a foldout bed, tiny sink, solar panels and storage tucked into every available corner. Their closet fits under the bed. Their kitchen is smaller than a restaurant prep station. Their backyard changes weekly.

They have parked near red-rock canyons, lakeside forests and desert pullouts where the stars seem close enough to touch.

But van life, they said, is not the effortless dream sometimes portrayed online.

“There are beautiful mornings,” Jenna said. “There are also nights when you’re trying to find a legal place to park, your water tank is empty and everything you own feels damp.”

The couple works remotely when cell service allows, planning routes around Wi-Fi, weather and public lands. They have learned to be patient with each other in a space where one person cannot cook while the other stands up.

“It makes your relationship very honest,” Miles said. “There’s no storming off to another room.”

## Downsizing after decades of accumulation

For many older Americans, moving into an RV is less about wanderlust and more about reclaiming control.

After their children left home, Linda and Paul Mercer looked around their four-bedroom house and realized they used only a fraction of it. The rest was filled with furniture, boxes and the weight of years spent maintaining a property that no longer fit their lives.

So they sold the house, donated much of what they owned and moved into a 30-foot RV.

“At first, it was emotional,” Linda said. “Every drawer had memories in it. But then it became freeing.”

The Mercers now spend part of the year near grandchildren and part of the year exploring national parks. Their monthly expenses are lower, though not nonexistent. Fuel, campground fees, insurance and repairs can add up quickly.

Paul said the biggest adjustment was psychological.

“In a house, you can keep things ‘just in case,’” he said. “In an RV, ‘just in case’ takes up space you need for everyday life.”

Their new home has made them more intentional, they said — about purchases, routines and time.

“We didn’t downsize our life,” Linda said. “We downsized the stuff around it.”

## A family choosing debt-free living

For the Carter family, moving into an RV was a financial decision first.

With student loans, medical bills and rising rent, the family of four felt stuck. Buying a traditional home seemed out of reach. Renting meant watching money disappear each month without building stability.

So they made a choice that friends called brave, risky and, occasionally, impossible: They sold most of their belongings, paid off consumer debt and moved into a fifth-wheel RV.

Their children share a compact sleeping area. Schoolwork happens at the dinette. Rainy days require creativity. There is no playroom, no garage and no space for clutter to spread.

But the Carters say the arrangement allowed them to live debt-free and spend more time together.

“We had to ask what we wanted our kids to remember,” said mother Rachel Carter. “A big house we were stressed about paying for? Or parents who had time and energy?”

The family budgets carefully, cooks most meals at home and chooses campgrounds based on cost, safety and access to work. Their life is not a vacation, Rachel said. It is still laundry, dishes, bills and bedtime routines — just in a smaller footprint.

Her husband, Daniel, said the biggest surprise has been how quickly the RV began to feel normal.

“Kids don’t need as much as we think,” he said. “They need security, routine and attention. We can give them that here.”

## The price of living small

Tiny living is often romanticized, but those who do it say it requires tradeoffs.

There is less privacy. Mechanical problems can become housing emergencies. Zoning laws, parking restrictions and marina rules can make stability difficult. Extreme weather feels more personal when walls are thin, roofs are low and water lines can freeze.

And while smaller homes can reduce expenses, they are not always cheap. A reliable RV or boat can cost tens of thousands of dollars. Repairs can be unpredictable. Remote work is not available to everyone.

Still, for people who choose these lives, the benefits can be profound: lower costs, less clutter, more mobility and a sharper sense of what matters.

Sociologists and housing advocates say the trend reflects both aspiration and necessity. Some people are choosing minimalism. Others are adapting to an economy in which traditional housing feels increasingly unattainable.

For Hale, the former circus train worker, the lesson of small-space living has stayed with him even after leaving the road.

He now rents a modest studio apartment. It feels spacious compared with his old train bunk. But he still owns little, keeps his shoes by the door and feels restless when he stays in one place too long.

“Living small taught me that home isn’t about how much space you have,” he said. “It’s about whether the life you’re living fits inside it.”

(CNN) -- Kate Meinhardt felt like a clown jammed into a Volkswagen bug the first time she tried to make dinner in her 240-square-foot apartment.

To open the oven, she had to fold a chair. To reach the refrigerator, she had to step sideways past a stack of books. And if a guest came over, the bed had to disappear into the wall before anyone could sit down.

“It’s a puzzle,” Meinhardt said. “Every object has to earn its place.”

Across the country, readers who shared their stories through iReport described a similar balancing act: families, couples and single residents making homes in spaces that test patience, creativity and sometimes relationships. Their apartments, cabins, converted garages and spare rooms may be small, but the lives inside them are anything but.

In New York, one iReporter described sharing a studio with a partner, a dog and a work-from-home setup squeezed between the kitchen counter and the foot of the bed. The couple’s dining table doubles as a desk, a laundry-folding station and, on weekends, a place for board games. Privacy, they said, is less about walls than headphones and agreed-upon silence.

In San Francisco, another contributor said her tiny in-law unit taught her to treat vertical space like real estate. Pots hang from the ceiling. Shoes live in a narrow rack behind the door. Seasonal clothes are sealed in bags under the bed. “If something comes in,” she wrote, “something else has to go out.”

For some, tight quarters are a choice. A family in Oregon told iReport they moved into a compact cabin to cut expenses and spend more time outdoors. Their children share a loft, toys are limited to a few bins, and the porch functions as a second living room when the weather cooperates.

For others, it is necessity. A recent graduate in Boston said rising rents pushed him into a room barely large enough for a twin mattress and a dresser. He keeps most belongings in labeled boxes and eats many meals at a library or coffee shop. “Home is where I sleep,” he said, “but the city is where I live.”

The stories reveal a common theme: small spaces require rules. No impulse purchases. No “junk drawer” that grows into a junk closet. No leaving things “just for now,” because there is no spare corner for “just for now” to hide.

Yet many iReport contributors said living small has changed the way they think about comfort. They have learned the value of light, good storage, multipurpose furniture and neighbors who understand the sounds that travel through thin walls. They have also learned that clutter can feel louder than noise.

Meinhardt, for her part, said she has stopped apologizing for the size of her apartment. When friends visit, she turns the bed into a sofa, clears the counter and lights a candle near the window.

“It’s not big,” she said. “But it’s mine. And somehow, when people are laughing in here, it doesn’t feel small at all.”

# The Art of Living Small: Lessons from People Who Downsized Their Lives

At first glance, minimalist living can look like a design trend: white walls, bare countertops, a carefully folded linen shirt. But for people who have truly downsized—into train cars, sailboats, camper vans, and RVs—minimalism is less about aesthetics and more about decisions.

What stays? What goes? What do you actually use? What makes a place feel like home when your home moves?

Across these radically compact lifestyles, one theme comes up again and again: having less space often creates more room—for freedom, clarity, travel, and relationships.

## Life on a Circus Train: “Everything Had to Earn Its Place”

For performers and crew members living on a circus train, downsizing is not a weekend decluttering project. It is a way of life built into the rhythm of the rails.

“When your home is a train car, you learn very quickly what matters,” says Lena, an aerialist who spent several seasons traveling with a circus. “I had one trunk for costumes, one shelf for books, and a little drawer for everything else. If I bought something new, something old usually had to leave.”

Her room was narrow, with a bed, a small vanity, and storage tucked into every possible corner. At first, she missed having options: different coats, extra shoes, a real kitchen. But the limitations became oddly comforting.

“There was no room for imaginary lives,” she says. “You couldn’t keep a cocktail dress for a party you might attend someday or hiking boots for a trip you might never take. Your belongings had to match the life you were actually living.”

The circus train also changed her understanding of community. Privacy was limited, but companionship was constant. Meals were shared. Tools were borrowed. Someone always had thread, tape, or a story from the last town.

“Minimalism sounds lonely when people describe it as getting rid of things,” Lena says. “But on the train, having less meant relying on people more. That was the best part.”

## A 25-Foot Sailboat: “The Ocean Is Your Living Room”

For Mark and Elise, moving onto a 25-foot sailboat began as a financial decision. Rent was rising, their jobs had become remote, and the idea of spending evenings at a marina felt romantic. The reality was more complicated.

“On a boat, you don’t declutter once,” Mark says. “You declutter constantly. Every grocery trip is a storage puzzle. Every object has to be secured before you sail. If you leave a coffee mug out, the boat will remind you.”

Their sailboat has a tiny galley, a compact berth, and storage under cushions and behind panels. Clothes are rolled instead of folded. Cookware nests inside other cookware. Books are limited to a small rotating stack.

Elise laughs when asked what she misses most. “A bathtub. And doors. Real doors.”

But she says the tradeoff is worth it.

“The ocean is your living room,” she says. “We don’t have a big couch, but we have sunsets. We don’t have a dining room, but we’ve eaten dinner under more stars than I can count.”

Living aboard also made them more conscious of consumption. Water, electricity, trash, and fuel are not abstract utilities; they are measured, carried, stored, and managed.

“You become aware of your footprint because you can literally see it,” Mark says. “Your water tank runs low. Your trash bag fills up. Your batteries drain. It teaches you limits in a very practical way.”

## A Camper Van in Europe: “We Collect Mornings, Not Things”

In Europe, van life often means waking up beside alpine lakes, parking near medieval villages, and learning the rules of each country one border at a time. For Sofia and Daniel, who travel in a converted camper van, downsizing was a deliberate rejection of routine.

“We didn’t want to spend our best years waiting for vacation,” Sofia says. “So we built a life that feels a little like vacation, even when we’re working.”

Their van includes a bed platform, small kitchenette, storage cubbies, a solar setup, and just enough room for two people to stand if they coordinate their movements carefully. They each own a small bin of clothing. Their kitchen has one pan, one pot, two mugs, and a sharp knife Daniel describes as “the most important member of the household.”

The couple has learned to embrace repetition. They wear the same outfits often. They cook simple meals. They choose experiences over souvenirs.

“We collect mornings, not things,” Daniel says. “A misty morning in Slovenia, coffee in Portugal, church bells in Italy—that’s what we bring with us.”

Still, van life is not all scenic overlooks and perfect photographs. There are rainy days when damp laundry hangs everywhere, nights spent searching for legal parking, and occasional arguments caused by the sheer lack of personal space.

“When you live in a van, you can’t storm off to another room,” Sofia says. “There is no other room. You have to learn to communicate, apologize, and sometimes take a walk.”

Minimalism, for them, has become less about owning the fewest things and more about removing friction.

“If something makes daily life harder, we don’t keep it,” Sofia says. “That includes objects, habits, and sometimes expectations.”

## RV Living: “Home Is a System, Not a Size”

RVs occupy a unique place in the downsizing world. They offer more space than a van or sailboat, but still demand discipline. For retirees, remote workers, traveling nurses, seasonal workers, and families, RV living can be both economical and expansive.

Janice, who moved into a 32-foot RV after her children left home, says the transition forced her to confront decades of accumulation.

“I had boxes in the garage I hadn’t opened in fifteen years,” she says. “At first, every item felt sentimental. Then I realized the memory wasn’t in the casserole dish or the old curtains. The memory was mine.”

She kept photo albums, a few heirloom recipes, her favorite quilt, and one set of dishes. The rest was sold, donated, or given to family.

“The surprise was how light I felt afterward,” Janice says. “I thought I was losing my history. Instead, I found I could carry it without carrying all the stuff.”

For Marcus and Renee, who live full-time in an RV with their two children, minimalism is about organization as much as reduction.

“Home is a system, not a size,” Marcus says. “If every shoe, toy, charger, and cereal box has a place, the RV feels peaceful. If one thing doesn’t have a place, chaos spreads fast.”

Their children each have a small bin for toys. When the bin is full, they choose what to donate before adding anything new. The family spends much of its time outdoors, treating campsites, parks, and trails as extensions of their home.

Renee says the lifestyle has changed the family’s values.

“Our kids don’t ask for as much stuff as they used to,” she says. “They ask where we’re going next.”

## The Emotional Work of Downsizing

Downsizing is often described in practical terms: square footage, storage hacks, capsule wardrobes, multi-use furniture. But the people who do it successfully tend to speak about the emotional side first.

Letting go of possessions can stir up grief, guilt, nostalgia, and fear. Objects represent identities: the person we used to be, the person we hoped to become, the life we thought we were supposed to want.

A woman leaving a house for an RV may not simply be donating dishes; she may be saying goodbye to the role of holiday host. A couple moving onto a sailboat may not simply be selling furniture; they may be stepping away from the assumption that adulthood requires a fixed address. A performer on a circus train may learn that home is not permanence, but belonging.

Minimalism asks uncomfortable questions:

- Do I own this because I use it, or because I feel guilty letting it go?
- Am I keeping this for my real life or an imagined one?
- Does this object support my freedom or limit it?
- What would I choose if space were precious?

For people living small, space is always precious.

## What Small-Space Dwellers Know

Despite their different homes, the circus performer, sailors, van travelers, and RV families share several hard-won lessons.

First, storage is not the same as space. Cramming every cabinet full does not make a tiny home livable; it makes it stressful. Empty space, even a little, is valuable.

Second, multi-purpose items are essential. A bench with storage, a table that folds down, a pan that can cook almost anything—these are not conveniences but foundations.

Third, maintenance matters. In a large house, clutter can hide. In a van, boat, train compartment, or RV, every mess becomes immediate. Minimalist living requires regular resets.

Fourth, the outdoors becomes part of the home. People who live small often do not experience their homes as confined because they expand into marinas, forests, town squares, beaches, campgrounds, and communal spaces.

Finally, minimalism is personal. It does not require owning a specific number of items or living in a photogenic white box. A minimalist life on a circus train may include sequined costumes. A minimalist sailboat may have three carefully chosen books. A minimalist RV may still carry a beloved cast-iron skillet. The point is not deprivation. The point is intention.

## More Freedom, Fewer Things

The promise of downsizing is not that life becomes easy. In many ways, small living is less convenient. You may have to convert your bed into a table, monitor your water tank, search for parking, repair leaks, or give up the luxury of closing a door.

But the reward is a life stripped closer to its essentials.

Lena, the aerialist, remembers standing between train cars late at night as the circus traveled through dark countryside. “Everything I owned was behind me in one small room,” she says. “And somehow I didn’t feel poor. I felt free.”

That freedom is the real appeal of minimalist living. Not empty shelves for their own sake. Not austerity. Not perfection. But the possibility that when we release what we do not need, we make space for what we do: movement, beauty, connection, and a clearer sense of home.

# Living in tight quarters  
### Families and individuals trade traditional homes for smaller, mobile spaces — and find out what “home” really means

For years, the dream looked familiar: a house with extra bedrooms, a garage, a yard and enough storage to hold decades of things. But for a growing number of people, home is becoming something smaller — and often, something with wheels.

Across the country, individuals and families are downsizing from conventional homes into vans, RVs, buses and tiny houses. Some are chasing financial freedom. Others want to travel, simplify, or live closer to nature. The trade-offs are real: limited privacy, fewer possessions and constant problem-solving. But for many, the smaller space has created room for something else.

Here are several stories from people learning to live large in tight quarters.

---

## The family that took the road instead of the cul-de-sac

When Marcus and Elena Rivera sold their three-bedroom home, they expected to feel grief. Instead, Elena says, the strongest feeling was relief.

“We had rooms we barely used and closets full of things we forgot we owned,” she said. “The house looked like success, but it felt like pressure.”

The couple now lives with their two children in a renovated 32-foot motorhome. The kids’ bunks are tucked into the rear of the RV, while the main living area converts from schoolroom to dining room to movie night space, depending on the hour.

Their mornings often start in national forests or campground parking lots. Marcus works remotely in software support, usually from a compact desk wedged beside the driver’s seat. Elena homeschools the children and plans travel around historical sites, state parks and libraries.

The biggest adjustment has been noise.

“There’s no ‘go to your room’ in the same way,” Marcus said. “If someone is having a bad day, everyone knows.”

But the family says the lack of space has forced them to communicate more directly. The children each keep one small bin of toys. Clothes are limited to what fits in a narrow cabinet. Souvenirs are usually postcards, pressed pennies or photos.

“We don’t buy much because there’s nowhere to put it,” Elena said. “That sounds restrictive, but it’s actually freeing.”

---

## A retiree finds a second act in a tiny house

At 68, Linda Cho didn’t want to spend retirement maintaining a house she no longer needed.

After her husband died and her adult children moved out, the family home became too quiet — and too expensive. Heating unused bedrooms and keeping up with repairs began to feel impractical. So Linda sold the house and moved into a 280-square-foot tiny home on wheels parked on a friend’s rural property.

Her new home has a sleeping loft, a compact kitchen, a small bathroom and a front porch just wide enough for a chair and potted herbs.

“I thought downsizing would feel like losing my past,” she said. “Instead, I kept the pieces that mattered.”

Linda’s belongings now fit into carefully planned spaces: family photos on one wall, quilts folded beneath the sofa, her late husband’s fishing hat hanging by the door. She donated, sold or gave away most of the rest.

The home costs less to heat, less to furnish and less to clean. That leaves Linda with more money for what she calls “the fun fund” — trips to visit grandchildren, pottery classes and the occasional weekend at the coast.

Still, tiny living has its challenges. The loft ladder is manageable now, she says, but she knows it may not be forever. She’s already considering modifications, including a downstairs bed and wider steps.

“A small house has to change as you change,” Linda said. “That’s the practical side people don’t always talk about.”

---

## The couple who built a school bus into a home

To outsiders, Jordan and Maya Ellis’ home still looks a little like what it used to be: a yellow school bus. But inside, the rows of seats have been replaced by wood countertops, solar panels, a composting toilet, a queen bed and a small kitchen with a two-burner stove.

The couple spent 14 months converting the bus themselves while living in a rented room and saving money. They watched online tutorials, learned basic electrical work and made plenty of mistakes.

“We built one cabinet three times,” Jordan said. “The first version fell apart, the second one didn’t fit, and the third one finally worked.”

Now the bus is their full-time home. They move with the seasons, spending winters in warmer climates and summers near mountains, lakes or family.

Maya, a freelance graphic designer, says the bus gave them a way to avoid high rent while paying down debt.

“It wasn’t just about travel,” she said. “It was about not feeling trapped by bills.”

But bus life can be unpredictable. Mechanical repairs are expensive. Parking laws vary widely. Internet access can make or break a workday. And the romance of waking up in beautiful places often comes with less glamorous realities: dumping tanks, tracking battery levels and finding safe overnight spots.

“You learn that freedom has logistics,” Maya said.

---

## A single dad turns a van into stability

For Anthony Brooks, van life wasn’t originally about adventure. It was about staying afloat.

After a divorce and a rent increase, Anthony began looking for a way to maintain custody time with his 9-year-old daughter while cutting costs. He bought a used cargo van and spent weekends turning it into a simple camper with a fold-out bed, storage benches, a portable fridge and blackout curtains.

He still works full time as an electrician and parks mostly on private property with permission — sometimes at a relative’s home, sometimes near job sites, sometimes at campgrounds when his daughter stays with him.

“I know people picture van life as beaches and sunsets,” he said. “For me, it was math.”

The van is small, but Anthony says it has given him breathing room financially. He has paid off a credit card, built savings and started planning for a small piece of land.

When his daughter visits, they treat the van like a clubhouse. They cook simple meals, play cards and sleep under string lights he installed along the ceiling.

“She doesn’t care that it’s tiny,” Anthony said. “She cares that I’m present.”

He is careful to point out that mobile living isn’t a universal solution. It requires safety planning, reliable transportation, access to showers and bathrooms, and a support network. But for him, it has been a bridge.

“This isn’t my forever home,” he said. “It’s my right-now home.”

---

## The digital nomad who chose less space for more time

For Priya Nair, the shift began with a spreadsheet.

She was living in a one-bedroom apartment, working long hours in marketing and spending much of her income on rent in a city she rarely had time to enjoy. When her company went remote, she decided to test a different lifestyle: six months in a converted van.

That was two years ago.

Priya’s van is sleek and minimal, with a small sink, a platform bed, hidden storage and a rooftop solar setup. Her entire wardrobe fits into two packing cubes. Her office is wherever she can get a signal — a library, a café, a campsite picnic table or the passenger seat.

“I didn’t realize how much of my life was arranged around paying for space,” she said.

The hardest part, she says, is loneliness. Social media often shows the scenery, not the isolation of arriving in a new town where you don’t know anyone. Priya has built community through meetups, coworking spaces and other travelers, but relationships require more intention on the road.

“You can’t be passive about friendship,” she said. “You have to reach out.”

Still, she says the trade has been worth it. She hikes more, works fewer unnecessary hours and spends less time buying things she doesn’t need.

“My home is tiny,” Priya said, “but my days feel bigger.”

---

## Small spaces, big questions

People who choose mobile living often talk about freedom, but their stories show that freedom is rarely simple. It can mean lower expenses, but also fewer conveniences. It can bring families closer, sometimes too close. It can offer mobility, but also uncertainty.

Zoning rules, insurance, maintenance, health needs, internet access and safe parking can complicate the lifestyle. For families with children, schooling and privacy require planning. For older adults, accessibility can become a major concern. And for anyone living on the road, the difference between “adventure” and “instability” can depend on income, health and support.

Still, those who make it work say the lifestyle forces clarity.

In tight quarters, every object needs a place. Every purchase has consequences. Every conflict is nearby. There is less room to hide from clutter, habits or one another.

But there may also be more room for intention.

“We didn’t just downsize our house,” Elena Rivera said from the family’s RV. “We downsized the noise around our life. Now we pay attention to what we actually need.”

For these mobile homeowners, living small is not about having less of everything. It is about deciding what deserves the space.

# Big Lives, Small Spaces: Why More Americans Are Choosing Tiny Living — and What They Give Up

**By Staff Writer**

For some, home is a house with a garage, a yard and rooms to spare. For others, it is a bunk on a circus train, a sailboat cabin, a van parked beneath desert stars, an RV moving between campgrounds, or a compact home where every drawer, shelf and square foot has a purpose.

Across the country, a growing number of people are embracing life in tiny spaces — not merely as a financial necessity, but as a deliberate lifestyle choice. Their homes may be small, but the reasons behind them are expansive: freedom, mobility, lower costs, environmental awareness, simpler routines and closer relationships.

Yet tiny living also comes with real trade-offs. Privacy shrinks. Storage becomes a daily puzzle. Weather, mechanical problems and zoning rules can disrupt life quickly. And for families, couples and traveling workers, small-space living often requires constant cooperation.

The experiences of people such as **Kate Meinhardt of Ringling Bros.**, **Jim Smith aboard a sailboat**, **Spencer and Bryce Pearson in a van**, **Deborah Greant in an RV**, and **the Chervenka family** show both the appeal and the difficulty of making a life in limited square footage.

## A Life on the Move

For people whose work requires travel, tiny living can be less of a trend and more of a practical reality.

Kate Meinhardt, connected with **Ringling Bros.**, represents a world in which home and work are often closely intertwined. Circus life has long been associated with mobility, compact quarters and the ability to carry one’s life from city to city. In that setting, living small can create a sense of discipline and adaptability. Personal belongings must be limited to what can be stored, moved and used efficiently.

The benefit is clear: mobility becomes easier when life is not anchored to a large house full of possessions. For performers and traveling staff, the small-space lifestyle can support a career built around constant movement. It can also create a strong community atmosphere, as people living and working in close proximity often depend on one another.

But the challenges are equally real. There may be little separation between professional and personal life. Quiet time can be difficult to find. A small room or bunk may need to function as bedroom, closet, office and retreat all at once. For people on the road, maintaining routines — laundry, cooking, exercise, rest — requires planning.

Tiny living, in that sense, is not only about space. It is about rhythm.

## Home at Sea

For **Jim Smith**, life on a sailboat offers a different version of small-space living — one shaped by water, weather and self-reliance.

A sailboat can provide extraordinary freedom. The view changes without the need to pack boxes or hire movers. A person living aboard can travel by wind, anchor near coastal towns and maintain a close connection to the natural world. Energy and water use tend to become more deliberate. Space constraints encourage careful decisions about what is truly necessary.

But living on a boat is not the same as vacationing on one. Storage is tight. Moisture, salt, storms and maintenance are constant concerns. Mechanical or electrical problems can quickly become urgent. Simple tasks — cooking, showering, sleeping — may depend on the boat’s systems, the marina’s facilities or the weather.

For boat dwellers, tiny living demands technical knowledge as well as minimalism. The home is also a vessel, and the resident is often part homeowner, part mechanic and part navigator.

The reward is independence. The cost is vigilance.

## Van Life and the Search for Freedom

For **Spencer and Bryce Pearson**, living in a van reflects one of the most visible forms of modern tiny living. Popularized on social media, van life is often portrayed through scenic photographs: open back doors facing mountain ranges, compact kitchens beside beaches, cozy beds under string lights.

The reality is more complicated.

A van can offer affordability compared with rent or a mortgage. It can allow residents to travel, take seasonal work, visit national parks and avoid being tied to one location. For young couples, remote workers or adventure-seekers, it can be a way to prioritize experiences over possessions.

But the small size of a van magnifies everyday issues. Where do you park overnight? Where do you shower? How do you cook during a storm? What happens when one person wants solitude and the other is only a few feet away?

Couples living in vans often say the arrangement requires patience and communication. Chores must be shared. Clutter cannot be ignored. A disagreement that might feel minor in a larger home can feel much bigger in a space where no one can simply go to another room.

Van living also depends heavily on access — to safe parking, public lands, campgrounds, Wi-Fi, water, fuel and repair services. When those are available, the lifestyle can feel liberating. When they are not, it can become stressful quickly.

## RV Living and the Middle Ground

For **Deborah Greant**, living in an RV represents another path into tiny living — one that often provides more amenities than a van while still preserving mobility.

Recreational vehicles can include kitchens, bathrooms, beds, heating, air conditioning and storage. For retirees, remote workers, traveling nurses, seasonal employees and people seeking lower housing costs, RV living can offer flexibility without giving up every comfort of a traditional home.

An RV can also provide community. RV parks and campgrounds often bring together people with similar lifestyles, creating informal neighborhoods that change from place to place. Residents may share advice on routes, repairs, weather and local services.

Still, RV life can be expensive in ways outsiders may not expect. Fuel, campground fees, insurance, repairs, propane and maintenance can add up. Large RVs can be difficult to park or maneuver. Smaller RVs can feel cramped during bad weather or long stays.

There is also uncertainty. Some communities restrict long-term RV living. Campgrounds may be full, seasonal or costly. Mechanical issues can threaten both transportation and housing at the same time.

For many RV dwellers, the lifestyle works best when paired with flexibility, savings and a willingness to solve problems on the road.

## Tiny Living as a Family

The challenges become more complex when tiny living includes children. The **Chervenka family** illustrates one of the most debated questions in the tiny-home movement: Can a family thrive in a very small space?

For families, the benefits can be significant. A smaller home may reduce housing costs, utilities and maintenance. Parents and children may spend more time together, sharing meals, chores and activities. With fewer rooms and fewer possessions, family life can become more intentional.

Tiny living can also teach children practical lessons about organization, conservation and cooperation. Toys, clothes and school supplies must be chosen carefully. Outdoor spaces, libraries, parks and community centers may become extensions of the home.

But families face unique pressures. Children need room to play, study and grow. Parents need privacy. Siblings may struggle with shared sleeping areas or limited personal space. Noise travels easily. A small home can feel cozy one day and crowded the next.

The success of family tiny living often depends on design. Foldaway furniture, loft beds, built-in storage, outdoor play areas and multipurpose rooms can make a small home more workable. Just as important are household expectations: everyone must participate in keeping the space clean and functional.

## The Economics of Going Small

One of the biggest attractions of tiny living is financial. Traditional housing costs have risen sharply in many regions, pushing some people to look for alternatives. Tiny homes, vans, boats and RVs can offer lower upfront costs than conventional houses, though the savings vary widely.

A tiny lifestyle may reduce:

- Rent or mortgage payments  
- Utility bills  
- Furniture and household purchases  
- Property maintenance  
- Consumption driven by excess storage space  

But tiny living is not always cheap. Costs may include:

- Vehicle or vessel repairs  
- Land rental or campground fees  
- Marina fees  
- Fuel  
- Insurance  
- Solar panels, batteries and water systems  
- Specialized compact appliances  
- Storage units for belongings that do not fit  

Experts on small-space living often warn that the lifestyle should not be romanticized as automatically inexpensive. A poorly maintained RV, boat or van can become a financial burden. A tiny house may be affordable, but land, permits and hookups can be difficult or costly to secure.

## The Legal and Practical Barriers

Beyond personal adjustment, tiny-space residents often encounter legal obstacles.

Zoning laws in many communities set minimum home sizes or restrict where tiny houses can be placed. RVs and vans may not be allowed as permanent residences in certain areas. Boat dwellers may face marina rules limiting liveaboard slips. Even when people own a tiny structure outright, they may struggle to find a legal place to put it.

Parking is a major issue for van and RV residents. Some cities have cracked down on overnight vehicle dwelling, citing safety, sanitation or neighborhood concerns. Advocates argue that such restrictions make life harder for people seeking affordable alternatives or experiencing housing insecurity.

Access to mail, health care, schooling, voting registration and insurance can also become complicated without a conventional address.

## Less Stuff, More Intention

Despite the obstacles, many tiny-space residents say the lifestyle changes how they think about possessions.

In a conventional home, unused items can disappear into closets, basements and spare rooms. In a tiny space, every object competes for room. Clothing, cookware, books, tools and keepsakes must justify their presence.

That can be stressful at first. Downsizing often means giving away, selling or storing items with emotional value. But it can also be freeing. Residents frequently describe feeling less burdened by clutter and more aware of what they actually use.

The lifestyle encourages questions many people rarely ask: How much space do I need? What do I own because I value it, and what do I own because I have room for it? What would I choose if I had to carry my life with me?

## The Emotional Side of Small Spaces

Tiny living is not only a logistical decision. It is an emotional one.

Small spaces can foster closeness, calm and simplicity. They can also intensify conflict, loneliness and fatigue. Bad weather can trap people indoors. Lack of privacy can strain relationships. Constant decision-making about water, power, parking or storage can become exhausting.

For solo residents such as those living on boats or in RVs, isolation may be a concern. For couples like Spencer and Bryce Pearson, togetherness must be balanced with independence. For families like the Chervenkas, the home must support both shared life and individual needs.

Successful tiny living often depends less on square footage than temperament. People who value flexibility, problem-solving and simplicity may adapt well. Those who need extensive privacy, large collections or predictable routines may find the lifestyle difficult.

## A Movement With Many Meanings

Tiny living is sometimes described as a single movement, but the people drawn to it are not all seeking the same thing.

For Kate Meinhardt and others connected to traveling performance, small-space living can be tied to work and community. For Jim Smith on a sailboat, it can mean independence and closeness to nature. For Spencer and Bryce Pearson in a van, it can represent mobility and adventure. For Deborah Greant in an RV, it can offer flexibility with familiar comforts. For the Chervenka family, it can be a way to simplify family life and rethink what home requires.

Their experiences point to a broader truth: tiny living is not about deprivation for its own sake. At its best, it is about choosing what matters most and designing a life around it.

But it is not effortless. It requires planning, adaptability, maintenance, legal awareness and emotional resilience. The smaller the space, the more important every decision becomes.

For those who make it work, the payoff can be large: lower costs, greater freedom, stronger relationships and a daily reminder that a meaningful life does not always require a big house.

Sometimes, it only requires enough room for what matters.
